analysis.one_liner: Retroactively stops lenders from chasing private student loan cosigners after a borrower's death or bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, never got a hearing or a vote, and drew no cosponsors before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law since 2018 stops private student loan lenders from declaring a default, demanding immediate payment, or collecting from a cosigner just because the student borrower died or filed bankruptcy, and requires lenders to release cosigners when the borrower dies. But those protections only apply to loans made after November 20, 2018. This bill would extend them backward to older loans, and would let loan holders sell the affected loans to the Treasury Department, which would retire the debt, so lenders are made whole for the money they can no longer collect.
analysis.who_benefits: Cosigners — usually parents or grandparents — on private student loans taken out before the 2018 protections took effect, where the student borrower has died or filed bankruptcy. Instead of inheriting the debt, they would be released from it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cosigners on older private student loans

how_it_helps.text: Makes the 2018 cosigner protections apply to private education loans signed before, on, or after the law's enactment, not just to newer loans.
Prohibits lenders from declaring a default or accelerating the debt solely because a cosigner died or filed bankruptcy, and requires release of the cosigner when the student borrower dies.
Creates a Treasury program to buy and retire affected loans from holders who show they were financially hurt by the change, with $5 million authorized for it.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders and holders of older private student loans lose the ability to collect from a cosigner after the borrower's death or bankruptcy. The bill offsets this by letting them sell those loans to Treasury, though the $5 million fund is small relative to the pool of affected loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private student loan holders and lenders

drawbacks.text: It rewrites the terms of loan contracts after they were signed; lenders that priced cosigner risk into older loans lose some of what they expected to collect, which the Treasury buyback only partly covers given its $5 million authorization.
The bill says Treasury 'shall' buy qualifying loans but authorizes only $5 million, so the program could be required to operate without enough money to purchase all applications.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protection is real and narrowly targeted: it stops debt collection from people who lost a child or a borrower's bankruptcy, which the 2018 law already deemed improper for new loans. The main cost falls on loan holders, who are partly compensated by a buyback program. The design is sound but the scope is modest — it touches only cosigner-protection provisions, not the balances owed by living borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never came back out; no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no cosponsors joined before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Angie Craig introduced the bill on May 11, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
That referral was the only action the bill ever received; it died in committee.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Holders of older private student loans, who kept the right to pursue cosigners for debts after a borrower's death or bankruptcy. No one else's situation changed.

for.name: Angie Craig
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill; it remained in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member of either party cosponsored the bill, so no partisan split shows in the record.

industries.industry: Private student loan holders and lenders
industries.note: The bill takes away their ability to collect from cosigners after a borrower's death or bankruptcy on older loans, but offers a Treasury buyback for holders who can show financial injury, with only $5 million authorized. Their interest in keeping those collections runs against the bereaved families and bankrupt cosigners the bill protects.
